title: He Tried to Set Limits on His State’s School Vouchers. Billionaires Helped Bankroll a Campaign to Unseat Him.
author: Henry Culvyhouse
content:
On a cold February morning at West Virginia’s Capitol, children in winter
jackets, holding signs and their homework, clogged the hallways outside the
House Finance Committee room. Delegate Vernon Criss, the committee’s
chairperson, popped outside his office, then promptly walked back in.

Five days earlier, the Republican lawmaker had proposed to limit payouts from
a voucher program that diverts public tax dollars to private education. Since
then, families had shown up each morning, and with them lobbyists and
organizers posting inflammatory assertions that the proposal would kill the
program.

Criss didn’t want that. Five years earlier, he voted to create the Hope
Scholarship program, the nation’s first educational savings account program to
have no income requirements. Since then, 11 other states have passed similar
legislation.

In the first year of the Hope program in West Virginia, it cost the state $9
million. Now, as 2026 was beginning, it was set to expand, with estimates that
it could cost $200 million or more a year. And Criss was concerned that
unchecked growth of the program, coupled with a spree of tax cuts, could put
the state budget into a tailspin. The state and its lawmakers needed “to face
the music,” as Criss would later say.

On that February day in Charleston, a staffer unlocked the committee door.
Parents and media filed in, taking seats along the narrow benches lining the
committee room’s walls. Kids lay on the floor. A delegate asked if the Hope
Scholarship bill would be discussed. When Criss said no, the parents and their
kids stood up and filed out.

Within the next few days, lawmakers would stop the effort to curtail spending
on vouchers. And Criss would soon be fighting for his political life.

![A man with white hair and glasses in a suit stands in a wooden doorway. A
group of people stand outside the door.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/CrissCommitteeRm2-20-26-crop.jpg?w=752)Criss greets
constituents supporting the Hope Scholarship. Perry Bennett/West Virginia
Legislature

The money and organizing behind the demise of the bill, as well as the
targeting of Criss, can be traced to “school choice” advocates at the local
and national levels and their ability to spend huge sums to have their way.

When Republicans assumed control of the West Virginia Legislature in 2015,
school choice — their preferred terminology for voucher-style programs —
became a rallying point for an array of political nonprofits. Through lobbying
and supporting sympathetic lawmakers, they helped establish the Hope
Scholarship six years later.

The first year, a [little more than 2,300 students enrolled in the
program](https://hopescholarshipwv.gov/Portals/HopeScholarship/content/Documents/Reports/Hope%20Scholarship%2022-23%20Annual%20Report.pdf?ver=b00P-zWfqfcR8bu4OzkZdg%3d%3d),
which was designed to permit more students over time. Today, [26,000 students
are taking part](https://wvtreasury.gov/About/Press-
Releases/details/treasurer-pack-welcomes-more-than-26-000-participants-to-the-
hope-scholarship-program-nearly-doubling-in-size), more than the enrollment in
the state’s largest public school district.

West Virginia has been part of a [nationwide push, partially funded by
billionaire-backed political
groups](https://www.propublica.org/article/education-department-public-
schools-activists-linda-mcmahon-trump), to use taxpayer dollars to fund
private schools.

Among the proponents of these programs are [the influential Koch family
network](https://apnews.com/article/7010023e5bb74e418de66b0660aff9c2) and
Pennsylvania billionaire Jeffrey Yass, who [has spent more than $350
million](https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/2025/12/05/jeff-yass-school-
choice-trump/) since 2015 on political campaigns, including a push for public
funding for private education.

In West Virginia, [Arkansas](https://www.propublica.org/article/arkansas-
private-schools-vouchers-delta-institute-developing-brain-autism-harm) and
[Texas](https://www.propublica.org/article/rural-republicans-school-vouchers-
education-choice), proponents have been eager to challenge anyone who got in
the way, including fellow Republicans who voiced concerns. Basic guardrails or
efforts to cap spending have been met with intense resistance.

During the 2026 West Virginia primary, three political action committees spent
heavily on independent advertisements, targeting 10 incumbent Republicans.
They succeeded in ousting four, all of whom had disagreements with the
governor; most expressed reservations about the Hope Scholarship.

Their biggest victory was unseating Criss, the long-serving incumbent and
high-ranking Republican.

One of the three PACs working to defeat Criss is affiliated with the Koch
family. Yass has contributed to the two others: School Freedom Fund and the
Sugar Maple PAC. David McIntosh, president of School Freedom Fund and the
affiliated Club for Growth, was jubilant afterward.

“These elections are a warning to Republican leaders like Vernon Criss — if
you oppose school freedom, expect to be held accountable,” he wrote in a press
announcement at the time.

Criss had been unopposed in his 2024 primary. In 2026, the three PACs spent
more than $145,000 to help a 23-year-old defeat him.

Criss’ proposal to put financial limits on the Hope Scholarship program came
as West Virginia public schools arrived at a dangerous crossroads. The program
directs dollars away from public schools, adding to funding shortfalls created
by enrollment drops.

Since 2019, [70 public
schools](https://mountainstatespotlight.org/2026/06/30/school-closures-impact-
communities/) have closed throughout the state, with the system losing more
than 30,000 students. By the end of this school year, up to 20 more schools
could close.

During the same legislative session this year, when lawmakers passed emergency
legislation to help one school district stay open, there was little drama — no
crowds in the hallways or the galleries.

### The Rise of Hope

In 2021, as West Virginia lawmakers worked on the bill that would create the
Hope Scholarship, they got some help from the outside: a lobbyist and
political operative named Jason Huffman.

Huffman has been the director of Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia since
the mid-2010s. The group is part of the larger Americans for Prosperity, which
was set up by the billionaire industrialist David Koch and supported by his
brother Charles, longtime donors to conservative causes. Americans for
Prosperity advocates for low taxes, school choice and loosened environmental
regulations throughout the country.

In shaping the West Virginia legislation, Huffman said, one goal was to create
a school voucher program that other states could model. While other states had
already passed voucher-style programs, they hadn’t made them open to all
residents regardless of income.

![A man with combed-back hair and a beard, wearing a suit and silver watch and
slightly smiling at the camera.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/New-Headshot-JH_maxHeight_3000_maxWidth_3000.jpg)Jason
Huffman is the director of Americans for Prosperity-West Virginia. Courtesy of
Jason Huffman

Among those advocating in West Virginia were members of Cardinal Institute, a
homegrown conservative think tank. Founded in 2015, the group made public
funding for private schooling one of its first policy planks. Over the last
decade, Cardinal has received significant donations from organizations that
also have received funding from Koch entities and Yass.

To support the Hope legislation, Cardinal’s leaders distributed research,
published columns in newspapers and linked up with other groups, like
Americans for Prosperity and the Institute for Justice, which litigates
libertarian causes, to push the issue. They also found allies in parents who
wanted the financial flexibility to send their children to private schools or
teach them at home or in small clusters of like-minded families.

Katie Switzer, a mother of six, became one of Cardinal’s most reliable
advocates. She had started looking into schooling options after her second
child was diagnosed with a learning disability.

“I just felt like this doesn’t feel good to send my nonverbal child to a
school that you know isn’t really collaborative, and I don’t know what’s going
on when she’s there because she can’t tell me when she gets home,” she said.
The experience made her a proponent of alternatives to public school.

Her story appeared in some of Cardinal’s [promotional copy for the
bill](https://cardinalinstitute.com/katie/). She sat in on a video call
presentation featuring state Sen. Patrcia Rucker, a Hope Scholarship
proponent. She took to Facebook to tout the program.

And she stepped up when the Hope Scholarship was challenged in court by other
parents who argued the program would undermine funding for public schools.

Hope’s opponents in the case gained support from the state Board of Education,
which argued the program siphoned money away from public schools. On the other
side was the West Virginia attorney general, Patrick Morrisey, defending the
law and the state.

The Institute for Justice was looking to get involved, but it needed to find
somebody with standing in the case. Switzer and another parent signed up,
giving the firm the ability to file motions and argue in court. The Institute
for Justice has received $8.5 million from charities controlled by Yass over
nearly a decade.

The case went to the West Virginia Supreme Court, where the justices ruled 4-1
in favor of the program.

The ruling meant the Hope program had survived. It was good timing for
Morrisey. He was about to make a run for governor. When Morrisey waded into a
tough four-way primary battle, the Club for Growth Action, a super PAC Yass
has donated heavily to over the years, was ready to help.

“Our goal in all of this is to elect people who will be champions for school
freedom, lower taxes, less regulation, so businesses can thrive,” McIntosh,
the group’s president, said in an interview.

The Club for Growth Action pumped $10.8 million into that race. Morrisey won
the plurality in the Republican primary and went on to trounce his Democratic
opponent in the general election.

On a cold morning in January 2025, Morrisey stood bundled up in a black wool
coat on the stairs of Capitol, its gold dome towering above him. He took the
oath of office and gave his address.

“We will expand the Hope Scholarship, putting more control in the hands of
parents to choose the best educational path for their children,” he said.

![A man with white hair wearing a blue coat stands outside at a wooden
lectern.](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/10/MorriseyInauguration1-13-25-crop.jpg?w=752)West
Virginia Gov. Patrick Morrisey at his inauguration ceremony in January 2025.
Club for Growth, which supports voucher-style programs, spent $10.8 million
through a super PAC to support Morrisey during the tough Republican primary.
Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislature

### Runaway Train

Hours before Morrisey gave his State of the State address earlier this year,
the House Education Committee called a meeting to hear about a report from the
Rand Corporation, a nonpartisan think tank.

Rand called on the state to fix what was becoming abundantly clear: Education
in West Virginia wasn’t just in transition; it was in crisis.

Initially the Hope Scholarship was limited to students attending public school
or children who would enter kindergarten. Participation grew over time. And as
the 2026-27 school year began, the program opened to any student in West
Virginia, including those who had spent their entire academic careers in
private school or in homeschooling.

That translated into tens of millions of additional state dollars to private
schools and homeschooling. Estimates for the 2026-27 school year ranged from
$230 million to more than $300 million in the months leading up to the
legislative session. The program costs for the year are still being tallied
but are currently projected at an unprecedented $150 million.

The Rand report suggested placing an income cap on the Hope Scholarship and
increasing funding for public schools.

While the Education Committee would work on public school funding, Criss’
Finance Committee would tackle the ballooning costs of the Hope Scholarship.
He was not interested in Rand’s solutions but found his own. By capping the
scholarship amount and limiting certain expenses, Criss was hoping he could
help prolong the program for families well into the future. But families would
soon be rallying against him.

In the time since the Hope Scholarship had withstood the court challenge,
Switzer’s reach had only grown. On
[Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/groups/hopeschoolerswv), she administered
a group that offers practical advice to hundreds of parents, or “Hope
Schoolers” as she called them, on questions like what items counted as
qualifying expenses and how to properly file for the program.

Before Criss’ plan rolled out, Switzer said she received word from a member of
the Finance Committee — though she did not disclose who — that the Hope
Scholarship would be discussed.

Writing a lengthy Facebook post, she warned that the move would severely
damage the program. “The bill takes away 19,000 children’s access to online
education, tutoring, private schools across state borders, and many other
beneficial academic programs,” she wrote.

Huffman, the Americans for Prosperity state director, took to radio and social
media to decry what he described as an existential threat to the program.
Parents with kids in tow echoed those fears.

Criss’ proposal would’ve capped the award amount for the Hope Scholarship at a
little more than $5,000 a year. He said his intent was to prolong the program
for the long run, not kill it.

### Read More

[ ![](https://www.propublica.org/wp-
content/uploads/2026/09/DSC_4111-edit_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=459&h=306&crop=1)
**We’re Reporters, Not Teachers. We Were Able to Start Private Schools
Anyway.** ](https://www.propublica.org/article/propublica-private-schools-
arkansas-west-virginia-north-carolina)

Huffman countered that by capping the award amount, inflation would eventually
erode families’ abilities to use the program for private education or
homeschooling.

Looking back, Criss said he anticipated some pushback, because the Hope
Scholarship is a “giveaway program.” He blamed political forces for riling
people up.

At a caucus meeting with the Republican supermajority — which holds 91 of the
100 seats in the lower chamber — Criss said he couldn’t muster the votes. A
bill to fix public schools that came out of the Education Committee died
entirely.

Election season was right around the corner, and Americans for Prosperity-West
Virginia and other groups hadn’t forgotten the Hope Scholarship battle. Criss
had failed what Huffman called “a litmus test” in trying to restrict public
money for parents looking for an alternative to public school.

Meanwhile, McIntosh, the president for Club for Growth, said he received word
from his allies in the Morrisey administration. Morrisey was concerned about
lawmakers who had opposed him on budget issues and school choice. The governor
was looking to replace those he saw as not aligned.

While the legislative backlash had been about one issue, the campaign against
Morrisey’s foes went well beyond education issues.

Ads depicted Criss as a liberal who wanted to open borders for illegal
immigration. That was based on a no vote Criss had cast against a piece of
legislation that would’ve mandated employers run [a citizenship check on every
employee](https://wvpublic.org/story/government/house-delves-into-deep-debate-
on-three-bills/).

Fliers mailed by the School Freedom Fund, a PAC affiliated with Club for
Growth, depicted candidates as supporters of drag queens. Americans for
Prosperity-West Virginia sent volunteers door to door to rally for their
candidates, including in Criss’ district.

The newly created Sugar Maple PAC — headed by a former state delegate and
Morrisey ally — ran ads accusing opponents of being Republicans in Name Only.

One mailer, depicting Criss driving a garbage truck, accused him of taking
“West Virginia’s values to the dump.” On the back, it reiterated his vote
against the citizenship check for employees and his vote against West
Virginia’s abortion ban.

“Vernon Criss’ liberal trash,” the flier read, with an image of black trash
bags.

![Criss is in the driver’s seat of a garbage truck. Large block type reads,
“Don’t let Delegate Vernon Criss take West Virginia values to the
dump.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Criss-Dump-
truck-1_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg?w=752)
![Two full garbage bags sit in the middle of an asphalt road. Large block
lettering reads, “Vernon Criss’ liberal trash” and “Dump Vernon
Criss.”](https://www.propublica.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Criss-Dump-
Truck-2_preview_maxWidth_3000_maxHeight_3000_ppi_72_embedColorProfile_true_quality_95.jpg)

Some of the mailers attacking Criss. PACs targeted him following his efforts
to rein in spending on the Hope Scholarship. Obtained by Mountain State
Spotlight

“I think that the fact that they called me a liberal, it just stuck out,”
Criss said. “You know, as the chairman of finance, I know that it’s a targeted
job, obviously, that’s part of the deal. Those types of things happen, that’s
just part of the politics involved here.”

The School Freedom Fund poured nearly $1 million into statehouse races across
West Virginia to both retain Morrissey’s supporters and oust detractors, like
Criss. Americans for Prosperity did the same, again targeting Criss, and
spending around $700,000 across the state.

A spokesperson for Morrisey said in an email that the governor is a supporter
of both public schools and the Hope Scholarship and “is also grateful that
organizations that share his worldview of helping West Virginia children
having the best educational opportunities in the country weigh in.”

Sugar Maple PAC and Yass did not respond to requests for comment. Yass
contributed $450,000 to Sugar Maple in the lead-up to the 2026 primary. Among
the three PACs, Sugar Maple spent the most on the Criss race: $86,000 to
attack Criss and $15,000 to back his opponent, Charles Hartzog, a 23-year-old
gas station cashier.

Criss didn’t just lose the primary; Hartzog beat him with 61% of the vote.
Criss is now running a long-shot campaign as a write-in for his district in
the general election.

### How We Tallied Spending

Mountain State Spotlight and ProPublica used filings from the West Virginia
secretary of state’s Campaign Finance Reporting System to analyze spending in
the 2026 state primary. For [Sugar
Maple](https://cfrs.wvsos.gov/public/committeeProfile?registrantID=1040003920),
[School Freedom
Fund](https://cfrs.wvsos.gov/public/committeeProfile?registrantID=1040003960)
and [Americans for
Prosperity](https://cfrs.wvsos.gov/public/committeeProfile?registrantID=1040002461)
committees, expenditures were compiled from Independent Expenditure Reports,
using a large language model. The output was manually reviewed for accuracy.
Duplicate and amended filings were omitted.
